subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is desertification?
options: The process by which fertile, semi-arid land gradually turns into desert
The natural spread of tropical rainforest into grassland
The flooding of low-lying coastal land by rising seas
The build-up of fertile new soil from river deposits
questions.explain: Desertification is the degradation of once-productive semi-arid land into desert-like conditions.

questions.q: Which region of Africa is most strongly associated with desertification?
options: The Sahel
The Congo Basin
The Cape region
The Ethiopian Highlands
questions.explain: The Sahel, on the southern edge of the Sahara, is the classic example of a region affected by desertification.

questions.q: How does overgrazing by livestock contribute to desertification?
options: It removes protective vegetation, leaving soil exposed to wind and water erosion
It adds too many nutrients to the soil, making it toxic
It increases rainfall, causing severe flooding of farmland
It cools the ground so that crops can no longer grow
questions.explain: Without plant cover, the bare soil is easily blown or washed away, accelerating land degradation.

questions.q: Why does rapid population growth increase the risk of desertification in semi-arid areas?
options: It raises demand for food and fuelwood, causing overcultivation and tree clearance
It reduces the number of farmers working the land
It automatically increases annual rainfall totals
It causes the land to become permanently waterlogged
questions.explain: More people place greater pressure on the land through farming and fuelwood collection, degrading the soil.

questions.q: A farmer in a semi-arid area clears trees for firewood and grows crops on the same plot every year without resting the soil. What is the most likely long-term outcome?
options: Soil fertility declines and the land becomes at risk of desertification
The soil becomes permanently more fertile each year
The area receives much heavier and more reliable rainfall
The land turns into dense tropical rainforest
questions.explain: Continuous overcultivation without fallow periods exhausts the soil and promotes desertification.

questions.q: A charity wants a cheap, appropriate-technology method to help Sahel farmers reduce soil erosion and trap rainwater. Which should it recommend?
options: Building lines of stones (stone bunds) across gentle slopes
Draining the soil with deep concrete channels
Irrigating the fields with seawater
Removing all vegetation before the rainy season
questions.explain: Stone lines slow surface runoff so water infiltrates and soil is held in place, a low-cost appropriate technology.

questions.q: How does planting trees (afforestation) help to reduce desertification?
options: Roots bind the soil and the canopy shelters the ground, reducing erosion
Trees stop all rain from reaching the soil, keeping it dry
Trees remove nutrients so that no plants can grow
Trees increase wind speeds across the land surface
questions.explain: Tree cover stabilises the soil and shields it from wind and rain, helping to reverse land degradation.

questions.q: Which is the world's largest tropical rainforest?
options: The Amazon rainforest
The Congo rainforest
The Daintree rainforest
The Taiga forest
questions.explain: The Amazon, mainly in Brazil, is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth.

questions.q: Which activity is the leading direct cause of deforestation in the Amazon?
options: Clearing land for cattle ranching
Building ski resorts
Planting coniferous plantations
Draining land for rice paddies
questions.explain: Clearance for cattle pasture is the single largest driver of Amazon deforestation.

questions.q: Why does deforestation often lead to increased soil erosion?
options: Tree roots and canopy no longer protect the soil from heavy rainfall and runoff
The soil becomes frozen once trees are removed
Removing trees adds a thick layer of new topsoil
Fewer trees means much less rain falls on the land
questions.explain: Without the trees intercepting rain and binding the soil, heavy rainfall rapidly washes the exposed soil away.

questions.q: In a tropical rainforest, where is the largest store of nutrients found?
options: In the biomass (living vegetation)
Deep within the bedrock
In the atmosphere above the canopy
In permanently frozen subsoil
questions.explain: Rainforest nutrients are held mainly in living plants and cycle quickly, so clearing the trees removes most of the nutrient store.

questions.q: Which of these is a sustainable way of managing a tropical rainforest?
options: Selective logging of mature trees
Clear-felling large blocks of forest
Converting forest to soya plantations
Flooding the forest to build a HEP reservoir
questions.explain: Selective logging removes only some trees, allowing the forest to recover and remain productive.

questions.q: What is agro-forestry?
options: Growing crops and trees together on the same land
Removing all trees to create large open fields
Farming fish in cleared rainforest rivers
Mining minerals from beneath the forest floor
questions.explain: Agro-forestry combines trees with crops so the land yields food while retaining tree cover and soil protection.

questions.q: A government wants to earn income from its rainforest without cutting it down. Which strategy best achieves this?
options: Developing ecotourism
Expanding commercial cattle ranching
Granting new large-scale logging licences
Opening open-cast mines in the forest
questions.explain: Ecotourism generates income from visitors while keeping the forest standing and intact.

questions.q: Which gas is the main greenhouse gas released by burning fossil fuels?
options: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Nitrogen
Helium
questions.explain: Burning fossil fuels releases large amounts of carbon dioxide, the principal human-produced greenhouse gas.

questions.q: Which human activity is the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions?
options: Burning fossil fuels for energy and transport
Recycling household waste
Planting new woodland
Building wind turbines
questions.explain: The combustion of coal, oil and gas for power and transport is the biggest source of human greenhouse gases.

questions.q: What is meant by the enhanced greenhouse effect?
options: Additional warming caused by human-produced greenhouse gases trapping more heat
The complete removal of all greenhouse gases from the air
The natural cooling of the planet during an ice age
The reflection of all sunlight back into space by clouds
questions.explain: Extra greenhouse gases from human activity trap more outgoing heat, intensifying the natural greenhouse effect.

questions.q: Which international agreement, signed in 2015, aims to limit the rise in global average temperature?
options: The Paris Agreement
The Treaty of Rome
The Schengen Agreement
The Berlin Accord
questions.explain: The 2015 Paris Agreement commits countries to limiting global temperature rise well below 2 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: Why does global sea level rise as the climate warms?
options: Melting land ice adds water and warming seawater expands (thermal expansion)
Warmer water shrinks and takes up less space
Rivers stop flowing into the oceans entirely
The oceans freeze over and push the water upwards
questions.explain: Sea level rises both because melting ice sheets and glaciers add water and because warmer ocean water expands.

questions.q: A country wants to cut its greenhouse gas emissions (mitigation). Which action best achieves this?
options: Generating more electricity from renewable sources such as wind and solar
Building sea walls to hold back the rising sea
Moving people away from flood-prone coasts
Improving early-warning systems for storms
questions.explain: Switching to renewables reduces fossil-fuel emissions, which is mitigation, whereas the other options are adaptation.
